title: Observability and the Software Supply Chain
subtitle: Trace the build system as a distributed service
summary: Pip’s market release stalls in CI and another rerun reveals nothing. Build pipelines are distributed systems too. Connected operations, shared context, and direct links from build results let feature owners investigate delays without becoming build-system specialists.

concepts.title: CI is also a distributed system
concepts.body: Pip’s slow build spends its time waiting for a runner. Webhooks, schedulers, workers, tests, and deployment machinery form a distributed workflow. A final pass or fail compresses those interactions. Pip traces the path to distinguish waiting from execution instead of repeatedly rerunning it.

concepts.title: Shared clients spread useful context
concepts.body: Pip adds commit, suite, and environment fields to build spans. Slack’s case uses shared instrumentation libraries for common dimensions and trace emission across CI services. Consistent context connects boundaries and comparable runs. Pip can group failures by the same suite and revision, not merely host health.

concepts.title: Bring evidence into the workflow
concepts.body: Pip opens a failed build result directly into its trace and suite query. Evidence belongs in interfaces developers already use. Preserved run identity and dimensions remove reconstruction work. Pip makes the investigation accessible to the feature owner rather than only the build specialist.

concepts.title: Compare changes and validate recovery
concepts.body: Pip reverts a suspected CI change and watches fresh runs. Slack’s examples connect cohort and revision comparisons with successive hypotheses and observations. A revert is an experiment, not proof of recovery. Pip verifies whether the affected failure pattern actually disappears after the intervention.

misconceptions.claim: This chapter is primarily about dependency vulnerability inventories.
misconceptions.correction: Its case concerns tracing and debugging CI/CD execution, including bottlenecks, failures, and changing behavior.

misconceptions.claim: A successful rerun explains why the original build failed.
misconceptions.correction: A rerun may restore progress while leaving the triggering condition and its recurrence risk unexplained.

scenario.title: Reruns hide a queue problem
scenario.context: Developers repeatedly rerun slow CI jobs, but most elapsed time precedes test execution.

options.label: Trace scheduling and runner allocation
options.benefit: Can distinguish queue delay from test runtime.
options.cost: Needs instrumentation across CI service boundaries.
options.consequence: The improvement effort can target scheduling capacity or coordination rather than the assertions.

options.label: Optimize individual tests first
options.benefit: May shorten execution for those tests.
options.cost: May barely affect total build time if waiting dominates.
options.consequence: Faster tests can leave developers waiting nearly as long for the build.

scenario.debrief: Measure where elapsed time is actually spent before choosing the optimization target.

quiz.question: A 20-minute build has two minutes of test execution. What should be investigated?
options: The application’s production latency, treating CI elapsed time as equivalent
Queueing and coordination along the build trace
quiz.explanation: The unexplained time may lie outside test execution in the distributed delivery system.

quiz.question: Which field supports comparing a regression across build runs?
options: Commit or revision identifier attached to relevant operations
A unique run ID without any reference to the source revision
The total number of tests across all revisions, without cohort dimensions
quiz.explanation: Revision context allows meaningful comparisons of changed code and resulting behavior.

quiz.question: A suspected change is reverted. What confirms the intervention helped?
options: The existence of the revert commit
Fresh affected runs no longer exhibit the observed failure pattern
quiz.explanation: Verification needs the same relevant outcome and population that motivated the intervention.
